Geometric models for algebraic suspensions

Aravind Asok ††thanks: Aravind Asok was partially supported by National Science Foundation Awards DMS-1802060 and DMS-2101898    Adrien Dubouloz ††thanks: Adrien Dubouloz was partially supported by Project ISITE-BFC ANR-15-IDEX-0008 ”Motivic Invariants of Algebraic Varieties” and ANR Project PRC “HQDIAG” ANR-21-CE40-0015-02    Paul Arne Østvær ††thanks: Paul Arne Østvær was partially supported by RCN Project no. 312472 “Equations in Motivic Homotopy Theory”
Abstract

We analyze the question of which motivic homotopy types admit smooth schemes as representatives. We show that given a pointed smooth affine scheme XX and an embedding into affine space, the affine deformation space of the embedding gives a model for the ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} suspension of XX; we also analyze a host of variations on this observation. Our approach yields many examples of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-(n−1)(n-1)-connected smooth affine 2​n2n-folds and strictly quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes.

Introduction

A very basic question in topology is: which homotopy types admit (smooth) manifold representatives? When a given homotopy type admits a manifold representative, one can then ask: can the homeomorphism (resp. diffeomorphism) types be enumerated? Broadly speaking, this note concerns algebro-geometric variants of such questions: we replace manifolds by smooth algebraic varieties (frequently affine) and the ordinary homotopy category by the Morel–Voevodsky 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category [MV99]. To guide the discussion, consider the following:

Question 1.
  1. 1.

    Which motivic homotopy types admit representatives that are smooth schemes?

  2. 2.

    If a motivic homotopy type admits at least one smooth representative, can one distinguish the isomorphism classes of distinct representatives?

An implicit impediment to making the above questions precise is the issue of specifying motivic homotopy types. The simplest motivic homotopy type, namely that of a point, admits many non-isomorphic representatives. We refer the reader to [AØ19] for a survey of results in this direction. For this reason, instead of trying to specify motivic homotopy types, we will focus on describing how such types can change. Here is a sample result.

Theorem 2 (See Theorem 3.2.1).

Assume BB is a scheme, 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is a BB-scheme, and π:𝔛→𝔸Bn\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} is a smooth morphism admitting a section ss. If, setting U:=π−1​(𝔸n∖0)U:=\pi^{-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0), the morphism π|U:𝔛|U→U\pi|_{U}:\mathfrak{X}|_{U}\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, then there is an induced (pointed) 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0,s⁡(0))∼(𝔛,s⁡(0)).{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge(\mathfrak{X}_{0},s(0))\sim(\mathfrak{X},s(0)).
Remark 3.

Theorem 2 is deduced from the more general result Theorem 3.1.1. Rather than stating this more general result here, let us explain the general principle at work. A smooth morphism π:𝔛→Y\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to Y will be called a generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence if there exists a dense open subscheme U⊂YU\subset Y such that π|U\pi|_{U} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. In that setting, the motivic homotopy type of 𝔛\mathfrak{X} can be obtained by gluing (as in [MV99, Theorem 2.21]) the motivic homotopy type of UU with the motivic homotopy type of 𝔛|Y∖U\mathfrak{X}|_{Y\smallsetminus U}. Under suitable additional hypotheses, we can control the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of the gluing.

Our next order of business is to create an ample supply of generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences to which our techniques apply. One source of such morphisms is provided by the deformation to the normal cone construction a la Fulton-MacPherson: the deformation space of an embedding of a smooth affine variety kk-variety in 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} will yield a family to which the preceding result may be applied. The following result is a straightforward consequence of the results above, combined with the Jouanolou–Thomason homotopy lemma.

Theorem 4 (See Corollary 4.1.6).

Suppose BB is a quasi-compact and quasi-separated (qcqs) base scheme. Assume (X,x)(X,x) is a finitely presented pointed smooth BB-scheme.

  1. 1.

    If the structure map X→BX\to B is furthermore affine, then for any integer i≥0i\geq 0, the motivic space Si∧𝔾m∧i∧XS^{i}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}i}}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X has the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of a pointed BB-scheme that is smooth and affine over BB.

  2. 2.

    If BB is affine and regular (e.g., the spectrum of ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} or a field), then the same statement holds for any BB-scheme XX that is smooth and has affine diagonal over BB (thus, any smooth separated BB-scheme satisfies the hypotheses).

Remark 5.

Theorem 4 can be viewed as a refinement and extension of the technique conceived in [ADF17]. In that paper, an inductive argument was used to show that the smooth affine quadric hypersurface Q2​n\operatorname{Q}_{2n} defined by the equation ∑i=1nxi​yi=z⁡(1−z)\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}=z(1-z) has the motivic homotopy type of the motivic sphere Si∧𝔾m∧iS^{i}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}i}} [ADF17, Theorem 2]. In retrospect, this smooth affine quadric is itself an iterated deformation space.

Construction 2.1.2 gives a generalization of the deformation to the normal cone construction. Loosely speaking, this construction lets us specify a degeneration locus ZZ in a suitable parameter space WW and then construct a morphism whose degeneration locus is precisely ZZ with control over the fibers over ZZ. Proposition 2.2.1 explains the relevant technical hypotheses that we will use to construct generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences. One reason for making Construction 2.1.2 in such generality is that we obtain a plethora of smooth scheme models of a given 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type. This flexibility allows us to encompass a large class of examples in affine algebraic geometry. Indeed, the problem of distinguishing isomorphism classes of smooth affine schemes within a given 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type contains many classical problems in affine algebraic geometry and the examples we construct.

The remainder of this note is then devoted to constructing several classes of examples. First, we generalize the results of [ADF17] in two ways: a) we construct new examples of highly 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected hypersurfaces by producing and analyzing a variation on Danielewski’s construction; for example, we construct many examples of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-(n−1)(n-1)-connected smooth affine 2​n2n-folds, b) we build new examples of strictly quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes. The problem of classifying 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-(n−1)(n-1)-connected smooth affine 2​n2n-folds is reminiscent of (a non-compact version of) that studied for manifolds by C.T.C. Wall in [Wal62]. Finally, we give examples to show that varieties that are not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible can become so after ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension; these results provide evidence supporting [AØ19, Conjecture 14].

Theorem 6 (See Theorem 4.4.1 and Remark 4.4.2).

If XX is a topologically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth complex surface that is not isomorphic to 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{{\mathbb{C}}}, then XX is not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, but for every integer N≥2N\geq 2, the space ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}\wedge X has the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of a smooth affine ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-scheme and is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.
