1 Preliminaries and Notation

Fix a base scheme BB; if we do not explicitly mention otherwise in the body of the text, the reader should not assume any additional finiteness hypotheses are imposed upon BB. Next, write SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B} for the category of schemes that are smooth over BB. For the convenience of referencing, we follow [Sta19, Tag 01V5] for our definition of smoothness as opposed to [Gro67, Definition 17.3.2]; note that, either way, objects of SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B} are locally of finite presentation over BB.

1.1 Simplicial presheaves and homotopy categories

Write SpcB\mathrm{Spc}_{B} for the category of simplicial presheaves on SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B}. We will typically use calligraphic letters to denote spaces. Objects of SpcB\mathrm{Spc}_{B} will be referred to as BB-spaces or simply spaces if BB is clear from context. The category SpcB\mathrm{Spc}_{B} has BB as a final object, and we write SpcB,∗\mathrm{Spc}_{B,\ast} for the category of pointed spaces, i.e., spaces 𝒳\mathscr{X} provided with a morphism B→𝒳B\to\mathscr{X} splitting the structure map. The forgetful functor SpcB,∗→SpcB\mathrm{Spc}_{B,\ast}\to\mathrm{Spc}_{B} has a left adjoint (−)+(-)_{+} of “adding a disjoint base-point”; this functor sends 𝒳\mathscr{X} to 𝒳+:=𝒳⊔B\mathscr{X}_{+}:=\mathscr{X}\sqcup B. Categorical constructions like ∧\wedge and ∨\vee will all occur in SpcB,∗\mathrm{Spc}_{B,\ast}, but sometimes we will explicitly indicate the base scheme BB (e.g., ∧B\wedge_{B}) for emphasis.

We view SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B} as a site by equipping it with the Nisnevich topology (in general, this is the topology generated by the Nisnevich c​dcd-squares). We write H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}) for the Morel–Voevodsky 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category: this category is constructed when BB is Noetherian of finite Krull dimension in [MV99], but we follow [Hoy14, Appendix C p. 3649] for the general case. While H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}) is described using the language of ∞\infty-categories in [Hoy14], one may also use model structures as described in [AHW17, §3.1, 4.1 and 5.1], [DRØ03, §2]. In brief, we realize H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}) as the left Bousfield localization of the injective Nis{\operatorname{Nis}}-local model structure on SpcB\mathrm{Spc}_{B} with respect to the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences. Isomorphisms in H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}) will be called 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences, and we write

[𝒳,𝒴]𝔸1:=HomH⁡(B)⁡(𝒳,𝒴),[\mathscr{X},\mathscr{Y}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{H}({B})}(\mathscr{X},\mathscr{Y}),

by analogy with homotopy classes of maps in topology.

Remark 7.

When BB is not Noetherian of finite Krull dimension, we caution the reader that the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category as defined here differs from the naive extension of Morel–Voevodsky’s definition; see [AHW17, Remark 3.1.4] for more details.

1.2 Cofiber sequences

We now collect for the reader’s convenience some well-known useful facts about cofiber sequences in pointed model categories. First, the motivic model structure we use is left proper, that is, pushouts of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences along cofibrations are again 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences. Left properness has the following useful consequence that we use repeatedly.

Lemma 1.2.1.

If f:(𝒳,x)→(𝒴,y)f:(\mathscr{X},x)\to(\mathscr{Y},y) is a morphism of pointed spaces and (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, then the canonical map

(𝒴,y)→hocofib⁡(f)(\mathscr{Y},y)\to\operatorname{hocofib}(f)

is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Next, we recall a general fact about the cofiber of a composite map (sometimes called the “octahedral axiom” as it gives rise to the octahedral axiom in triangulated categories).

Proposition 1.2.2.

If f1:𝒳2→𝒳1f_{1}:\mathscr{X}_{2}\to\mathscr{X}_{1} and f0:𝒳1→𝒳0f_{0}:\mathscr{X}_{1}\to\mathscr{X}_{0} are pointed morphisms of spaces, then there is a cofiber sequence of the form:

hocofib⁡(f1)⟶hocofib⁡(f0​f1)⟶hocofib⁡(f0)\operatorname{hocofib}(f_{1})\longrightarrow\operatorname{hocofib}(f_{0}f_{1})\longrightarrow\operatorname{hocofib}(f_{0})
Proof.

This is shown in [Hov99, Proposition 6.3.6]. ∎

The following fact has to do with smash products and base-points. Assume (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) and (𝒴,y)(\mathscr{Y},y) are pointed spaces. In this case, we may form the smash product 𝒳∧𝒴\mathscr{X}\wedge\mathscr{Y} in SpcB,∗\mathrm{Spc}_{B,\ast}. The base-point xx determines a canonical pointed map x:S0→𝒳+x:S^{0}\to\mathscr{X}_{+} sending the non-base-point of S0S^{0} to the point xx. Smashing this morphism with i​d𝒴id_{{\mathscr{Y}}} then defines a morphism

𝒴=𝒴∧S0⟶i​d∧x𝒴∧𝒳+.\mathscr{Y}=\mathscr{Y}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}S^{0}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle id{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}x}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathscr{Y}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}\mathscr{X}_{+}.

This morphism is split by the morphism 𝒳+→S0\mathscr{X}_{+}\to S^{0} that collapses 𝒳\mathscr{X} to the non-base-point. It follows that the displayed morphism is a cofibration in the injective local model structure since it is a monomorphism.

Proposition 1.2.3.

For any pointed spaces (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) and (𝒴,y)(\mathscr{Y},y), there is a canonical identification

hocofib⁡(𝒴⟶i​d∧x𝒳+∧𝒴)≅𝒳∧𝒴.\operatorname{hocofib}(\mathscr{Y}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle id{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}x}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathscr{X}_{+}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}\mathscr{Y})\cong\mathscr{X}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}\mathscr{Y}.
Proof.

Since the map in question is a cofibration, the homotopy cofiber coincides with the cofiber. The identification of the cofiber is an exercise in unwinding the definition of the smash product (for more details, see [ADF17, Proposition 2.2.4]). ∎

2 Deformation to the normal cone revisited

In this section, we study a variation on the “deformation to the normal cone” construction, which appears in many places; see, e.g., [FL85, §IV.5] or [Ver76, §2]. Our eventual goal will be to use this kind of construction to produce generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences π:𝔛→W\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to W with good control over the closed subscheme Z⊂WZ\subset W over which π\pi fails to be an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

2.1 Parameterized deformation spaces: construction

Henceforth, we assume BB is an arbitrary scheme. The deformation to the normal cone construction can be realized in terms of affine blow-ups. The theory of affine blow-ups has been worked out in great generality in [MRR20, §2] (see also [KZ99, Dub05b] for special cases), but we will recall what we need here.

2.1.1Affine blow-ups.

Assume Z⊂D⊂XZ\subset D\subset X is a triple consisting of a scheme XX, a closed subscheme ZZ defined by a quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals ℐ\mathscr{I} of ideals and a locally principal subscheme DD defined by a quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals 𝒥\mathscr{J} contained in ℐ\mathscr{I}. The affine blow-up BlZD⁡(X)\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}^{D}(X) is defined as follows: as usual, we write Blℐ⁡𝒪X\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathscr{I}}\mathscr{O}_{X} for the (graded) blow-up algebra ⨁n≥0ℐn\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathscr{I}^{n} [Sta19, Tag 052Q]. If we view the local generators of 𝒥\mathscr{J} as living in degree one, then BlZD⁡(X)\operatorname{Bl}_{Z}^{D}(X) is the complement of the variety V+​(𝒥)V_{+}(\mathscr{J}) defined by the homogeneous ideal 𝒥\mathscr{J} in Proj⁡Blℐ⁡𝒪X{\operatorname{Proj}}\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathscr{I}}\mathscr{O}_{X} [MRR20, Definition 2.1, Lemma 2.3]. With these preliminaries in mind, we introduce the following:

Construction 2.1.2.

Fix a base scheme BB. We assume given:

  1. 1.

    A smooth BB-scheme WW (“the parameter space”);

  2. 2.

    A locally finitely presented flat BB-scheme ZZ equipped with a closed immersion of BB-schemes i:Z→Wi:Z\to W (“the degeneration locus”);

  3. 3.

    A smooth BB-scheme YY;

  4. 4.

    A BB-scheme XX together with a surjective smooth morphism ψ:X→Z\psi:X\to Z, and a closed immersion f:X→Y×BWf:X\to Y\times_{B}W such that the diagram

    commutes; and

  5. 5.

    A locally principal divisor DD on Y×BWY\times_{B}W that contains Y×BZY\times_{B}Z.

The parameterized deformation space

π:D⁡(X,i,f)⟶W\pi:\operatorname{D}(X,i,f)\longrightarrow W

is the affine blow-up BlXD⁡(Y×BW)\operatorname{Bl}_{X}^{D}(Y\times_{B}W).

The next example justifies the terminology parameterized deformation space for the output π\pi of Construction 2.1.2.

Example 2.1.3.

Take W=𝔸B1W={\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}, fix a closed immersion of finitely presented smooth BB-schemes f:X→Yf:X\to Y, let Z=BZ=B, take i:Z→𝔸B1i:Z\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} the zero section, and let DD be the Cartier divisor Y×BZ⊂Y×B𝔸B1Y\times_{B}Z\subset Y\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}. In that case, if f′:X→Y×𝔸B1f^{\prime}:X\to Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} is the base-change of ff along the projection map Y×𝔸B1→YY\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}\to Y, then the structure morphism X→BX\to B fits into a commutative square as in Construction 2.1.2, and D⁡(X,i,f)\operatorname{D}(X,i,f) is the usual deformation space D⁡(X,Y)\operatorname{D}(X,Y) of the closed immersion ff.

2.2 Parameterized deformation spaces: structural properties

This subsection aims to control the structure of parameterized deformation spaces. In particular, we want to exhibit hypotheses under which the morphism π:D⁡(X,i,f)→W\pi:\operatorname{D}(X,i,f)\to W is smooth, and we would also like to control the structure of the exceptional locus. Indeed, if we take YY to be an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth BB-scheme, then as long as π\pi is smooth, it is automatically a generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence in the sense of the introduction.

In the setup of Construction 2.1.2, if Z⊂WZ\subset W is an effective Cartier divisor, then the fiber product Y×BZ↪Y×BWY\times_{B}Z\hookrightarrow Y\times_{B}W is an effective Cartier divisor as well; we will take D=W×BYD=W\times_{B}Y in the sequel and we write 𝒥\mathscr{J} for the ideal sheaf of Y×BZY\times_{B}Z in Y×BWY\times_{B}W. In that case, the closed immersion ψ:X→Z\psi:X\to Z necessarily factors through a closed immersion f′:X↪Y×BZf^{\prime}:X\hookrightarrow Y\times_{B}Z. We write ℐ\mathscr{I} for the ideal sheaf of XX in Y×BWY\times_{B}W and 𝒥X\mathscr{J}_{X} for the restriction of 𝒥\mathscr{J} to XX. In that case, we write 𝒞f′:=ℐ/(ℐ2+𝒥)\mathscr{C}_{f^{\prime}}:=\mathscr{I}/(\mathscr{I}^{2}+\mathscr{J}) for the conormal sheaf of f′f^{\prime} and 𝒩f′\mathscr{N}_{f^{\prime}} for its dual, i.e., the normal sheaf of the embedding.

We want to speak about regular immersions, but doing so in the context when our base schemes have no finiteness hypotheses imposed upon them requires more work. We refer the reader to [Sta19, Tag 067M] and [Sta19, Tag 0638] for discussions about regular immersion in this generality. We freely use the fact that regular immersions always have locally free (co)normal sheaves (combine [Sta19, Tag 067P] and [Sta19, Tag 063M]).

Since smooth BB-schemes are locally finitely presented by assumption, and since closed immersions are quasi-compact, it follows that a closed immersion of smooth BB-schemes is automatically finitely presented. Moreover, closed immersions of smooth BB-schemes are automatically regular immersions [Sta19, Tag 067U]. Consequently, any closed immersion of smooth BB-schemes has a well-defined normal sheaf 𝒩X/Y\mathscr{N}_{X/Y}, which is a finite rank locally free 𝒪X\mathscr{O}_{X}-module.

Proposition 2.2.1.

Assume (i:Z→W,ψ:X→Z,f:X→Y×BW)(i:Z\to W,\psi:X\to Z,f:X\to Y\times_{B}W) are as in Construction 2.1.2, and furthermore suppose ZZ is an effective Cartier divisor on WW.

  1. 1.

    The morphism π−1​(W∖Z)→W∖Z\pi^{-1}(W\smallsetminus Z)\to W\smallsetminus Z is isomorphic to the projection Y×B(W∖Z)→W∖ZY\times_{B}(W\smallsetminus Z)\to W\smallsetminus Z.

  2. 2.

    If the closed immersion f′:X→Y×BZf^{\prime}:X\to Y\times_{B}Z induced by ff is regular (e.g., if ff is regular), then the morphism π−1​(Z)→Z\pi^{-1}(Z)\to Z is the composite

    𝕍f′⟶pX⟶ψZ\mathbb{V}_{f^{\prime}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\longrightarrow}}X\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\psi}}{{\longrightarrow}}Z

    where pp is a torsor under the vector bundle associated to 𝒩f′\mathscr{N}_{f^{\prime}}.

  3. 3.

    If both ii and f′f^{\prime} are regular immersions (the latter happens if ff is a regular immersion), then

    π:D⁡(X,i,f)⟶W\pi:\operatorname{D}(X,i,f)\longrightarrow W

    is a smooth morphism; if YY is furthermore finitely presented, then so is π\pi.

Proof.

We set Y′=BlX⁡(Y×BW)Y^{\prime}=\operatorname{Bl}_{X}(Y\times_{B}W) and observe that π\pi factors as

D⁡(X,i,f)⟶Y′⟶Y×BW⟶W\operatorname{D}(X,i,f)\longrightarrow Y^{\prime}\longrightarrow Y\times_{B}W\longrightarrow W

where the first morphism is an open immersion, and Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y is an isomorphism on the complement of XX [Sta19, Tag 02OS]. The first statement then follows from [MRR20, Lemma 2.4] which states that the exceptional divisor of the affine blow-up, i.e., the pre-image of the center of the affine blow-up, coincides with the pre-image of Y×BZY\times_{B}Z.

It follows from the final observation of the preceding paragraph that the restriction of π\pi to ZZ also factors as the composite of the projection map from the exceptional divisor to the center of the blow-up followed by the map ψ\psi in 2.1.2. In that case, the second statement is [MRR20, Proposition 2.9(1)]; the assertion that the exceptional divisor is a torsor under a vector bundle follows by inspecting the proof of that result.

For the third statement, observe that the smoothness of π\pi under the stated hypotheses is [MRR20, Proposition 2.16(4)]. If YY is finitely presented, then Y×BW→WY\times_{B}W\to W is as well. In that case, π\pi is finitely presented by [MRR20, Proposition 2.16(1)]. ∎

Remark 2.2.2.

As observed in [MRR20, §2.3], all of the results in [MRR20, §2] hold under a weaker hypothesis than stated above. In particular, Proposition 2.2.1 holds replacing the regularity assumption on ii and f′f^{\prime} by H1H_{1}-regularity in the sense of [Sta19, Tag 063D].

Corollary 2.2.3 (Deformation to the normal cone).

If BB is a base scheme and i:X→Yi:X\to Y is a closed immersion of finitely presented smooth BB-schemes, the morphism π:D⁡(X,Y)→𝔸B1\pi:\operatorname{D}(X,Y)\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} (see Example 2.1.3) enjoys the following properties:

  1. 1.

    The morphism π−1​(𝔸B1∖0)→𝔸B1∖0\pi^{-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}\smallsetminus 0)\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}\smallsetminus 0 is isomorphic to the projection map Y×B𝔸B1∖0→𝔸B1∖0Y\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}\smallsetminus 0\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}\smallsetminus 0.

  2. 2.

    The BB-scheme π−1​(0)\pi^{-1}(0) is isomorphic to 𝕍i\mathbb{V}_{i}, the total space of the normal bundle to ii.

  3. 3.

    The morphism π\pi is a smooth morphism; if YY is finitely presented, then so is π\pi.

Proof.

We check the hypotheses of Proposition 2.2.1 are satisfied. Indeed, here we take i:Z→Wi:Z\to W as the closed immersion B↪𝔸B1B\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}, which is a Cartier divisor and a regular immersion. The map f′:X→Yf^{\prime}:X\to Y is also a regular immersion by assumption, and the result follows. The only thing that isn’t immediate is that 𝕍i\mathbb{V}_{i} is the normal bundle rather than a torsor under it. However, the exact sequence of conormal sheaves associated with the sequence of closed immersions X↪Y↪Y×B𝔸1X\hookrightarrow Y\hookrightarrow Y\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{1} is split by the projection Y×B𝔸1→YY\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to Y, so the final assertion follows from (the proof of) [MRR20, Proposition 2.9(2)]. ∎

Unwinding the definitions of blow-up algebras, it is frequently possible to write explicitly defining equations for the parameterized deformation spaces described above. In particular, one realizes that many varieties presented explicitly by equations can be realized in terms of the parameterized deformation space construction.

Example 2.2.4.

Assume B=Spec⁡kB=\operatorname{Spec}k is the spectrum of an arbitrary base ring kk and pick coordinates x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} on 𝔸Bn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B}. Assume that i:Z↪𝔸Bni:Z\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} is a closed immersion of BB-schemes defined by an element gg, that Y=Spec⁡RY=\operatorname{Spec}R is a smooth affine kk-scheme and that X′↪YX^{\prime}\hookrightarrow Y is a smooth closed subscheme defined by a regular ideal I=(f1,…,fc)I=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{c}). Then f:X=X′×BZ↪Y×B𝔸nf:X=X^{\prime}\times_{B}Z\hookrightarrow Y\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{n} is a regular closed immersion whose image is the smooth closed subscheme of Y×B𝔸BnY\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} defined by the regular sequence (f1,…,fc,g)(f_{1},\ldots,f_{c},g). The scheme Y×BZY\times_{B}Z is a Cartier divisor in Y×B𝔸BnY\times_{B}{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} cut out by the single element gg. Unwinding the definitions, we see that the affine scheme of Construction 2.1.2 is given explicitly by:

D⁡(X,i,f)=Spec⁡R⁡[x1,…,xn]​[I/g]=Spec⁡R⁡[x1,…,xn,t1,…,tc]/(f1−t1​g,…,fc−tc​g).{\mathrm{D}}(X,i,f)=\operatorname{Spec}R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}][I/g]=\operatorname{Spec}R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},t_{1},\ldots,t_{c}]/(f_{1}-t_{1}g,\ldots,f_{c}-t_{c}g).

2.3 The purity isomorphism

We will refer to a closed immersion of smooth BB-schemes X⊂YX\subset Y as a smooth pair. By a morphism of smooth pairs f:(X⊂Y)→(X′⊂Y′)f:(X\subset Y)\to(X^{\prime}\subset Y^{\prime}), we will mean a morphism of BB-schemes f:Y→Y′f:Y\to Y^{\prime} such that ff restricts to a morphism of BB-schemes X→X′X\to X^{\prime}. A morphism of smooth pairs is transversal if X=f−1​(X′)X=f^{-1}(X^{\prime}) and the induced map φ:𝒩X/Y→f∗​𝒩X′/Y′\varphi:\mathscr{N}_{X/Y}\to f^{*}\mathscr{N}_{X^{\prime}/Y^{\prime}} is an isomorphism. Having introduced the above notions, the homotopy purity theorem takes the following form (we state it here because we could not find the statement at this level of generality in the literature; the original statement is [MV99, §3 Theorem 3.23]).

Theorem 2.3.1 (Homotopy purity).

Given a smooth pair X⊂YX\subset Y in SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B}, there is a canonical isomorphism in H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}) of the form

X/(X∖Y)≅Th⁡(𝒩X/Y).X/(X\smallsetminus Y)\cong{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{X/Y}).

Given a transversal morphism of pairs f:(X⊂Y)→(X′⊂Y′)f:(X\subset Y)\to(X^{\prime}\subset Y^{\prime}), there is a homotopy commutative square of the form

where the vertical maps are induced by ff.

Proof.

This follows immediately from the proof of [Hoy17, Theorem 3.23]. There are two remarks to make: the additional hypotheses (implicitly) placed on BB in [Hoy17] stem from the presence of the action of a group scheme. Moreover, the fact that deformation to the normal cone construction has the required properties over an arbitrary base scheme BB follows from Corollary 2.2.3. The transversality hypothesis is precisely what is needed to obtain a morphism of Thom spaces; the classical functoriality statement may be found at [Voe03, Lemma 2.1]. ∎

3 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-homotopy types of generic weak equivalences

Fix a base scheme BB, and suppose WW is a pointed smooth BB-scheme. Recall from the introduction that a smooth morphism π:𝔛→W\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to W is called a generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence if there exists an open dense subscheme UU of WW such that π|U:𝔛|U→U\pi|_{U}:\mathfrak{X}|_{U}\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. For UU maximal with this property, we will refer to W∖UW\smallsetminus U as the degeneration locus of π\pi. Our aim is to describe the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of 𝔛\mathfrak{X} in terms of the degeneration locus W∖UW\smallsetminus U of π\pi.

3.1 Degenerations over a subscheme

The goal of this section is to establish the following result.

Theorem 3.1.1.

Fix a finitely presented, pointed, smooth BB-scheme (W,w)(W,w) that is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. Assume 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is a BB-scheme, and π:𝔛→W\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to W is a smooth morphism of BB-schemes admitting a section ss (point 𝔛\mathfrak{X} by s⁡(w)s(w)). Assume ZZ is a finitely presented smooth BB-scheme, i:Z→Wi:Z\to W is a closed immersion, and let j:U:=W∖Z→Wj:U:=W\smallsetminus Z\to W be the complementary open immersion. Write 𝔛|U\mathfrak{X}|_{U} for the restriction of 𝔛\mathfrak{X} to UU and π|U\pi|_{U} for the restricted morphism, and let i′:𝔛Z→𝔛i^{\prime}:\mathfrak{X}_{Z}\to\mathfrak{X} be the base-change of ii along π\pi. The morphisms ii and i′i^{\prime} are regular immersions. If the morphism π|U:𝔛U→U\pi|_{U}:\mathfrak{X}_{U}\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, then there is a split cofiber sequence

Th⁡(𝒩i)⟶Th⁡(𝒩i′)⟶𝔛,{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i})\longrightarrow{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}})\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X},

where 𝒩i\mathscr{N}_{i} and 𝒩i′\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}} are the normal bundles of the corresponding regular immersions.

Proof.

For notational convenience, we will suppress BB from the notation. Consider the section s:W→𝔛s:W\to\mathfrak{X}. By assumption, the restriction of ss to 𝔛U\mathfrak{X}_{U} coincides with the inclusion U→𝔛UU\to\mathfrak{X}_{U}. Since π|U\pi|_{U} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence by construction and since ss is a section of π\pi, it follows that s|Us|_{U} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence by the 22 out of 33 property for 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences. The section ss then induces a Cartesian square of the form

(3.1.1)

By assumption, the complementary closed immersions form a transversal morphism of pairs.

Note that 𝔛Z\mathfrak{X}_{Z} is smooth over BB since it is smooth over ZZ. Since Z→WZ\to W is a closed immersion of smooth schemes, it follows that the base-change of π\pi along ii, i.e., 𝔛Z→𝔛\mathfrak{X}_{Z}\to\mathfrak{X}, is a closed immersion of smooth BB-schemes. As a consequence, i′:𝔛Z→𝔛i^{\prime}:\mathfrak{X}_{Z}\to\mathfrak{X} is a regular immersion and thus has a well-defined normal sheaf 𝒩i′\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}}.

By homotopy purity in Theorem 2.3.1, there is thus an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence 𝔛/𝔛U∼Th⁡(𝒩i′)\mathfrak{X}/\mathfrak{X}_{U}\sim{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}}). Since the map U→𝔛UU\to\mathfrak{X}_{U} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, we also conclude that

hocofib⁡(U→𝔛)≅Th⁡(𝒩i′).\operatorname{hocofib}(U\to\mathfrak{X})\cong{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}}).

This description corresponds to computing the homotopy colimit of the morphism U→𝔛U\to\mathfrak{X} going along the left and bottom edge of (3.1.1).

Now, we compute the homotopy colimit of U→𝔛U\to\mathfrak{X} going around the top and right edge of (3.1.1). To this end, we appeal to Proposition 1.2.2, which tells us there is a cofiber sequence of the form

hocofib⁡(U→W)⟶hocofib⁡(U→𝔛)⟶hocofib⁡(W→𝔛).\operatorname{hocofib}(U\to W)\longrightarrow\operatorname{hocofib}(U\to\mathfrak{X})\longrightarrow\operatorname{hocofib}(W\to\mathfrak{X}).

The homotopy purity isomorphism applied to the closed immersion Z→WZ\to W shows that the first term in the above cofiber sequence is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to Th⁡(𝒩i){\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i}). Because WW is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, Lemma 1.2.1 implies that the last term is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to 𝔛\mathfrak{X} pointed by any point in the image of WW, e.g., s⁡(w0)s(w_{0}).

Combining all the observations above, we conclude that there is a cofiber sequence of the form

Th⁡(𝒩i)⟶Th⁡(𝒩i′)⟶𝔛.{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i})\longrightarrow{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{i^{\prime}})\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X}.

Note that the first map is split by π\pi and is thus evidently a cofibration; in fact, 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is the actual cofiber of the first map as well. ∎

Remark 3.1.2.

Suppose BB is qcqs base scheme, WW is a finitely presented smooth BB-scheme, and π:𝔛→W\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to W is a smooth morphism. Assume i:Z→Wi:Z\to W is a closed immersion with open complement j:U→Wj:U\to W. In that case, there is a homotopy cocartesian gluing square (see [MV99, Theorem 2.21] or [Hoy17, Theorem 4.18] for a statement in this generality) of the form

Unwinding the definitions, j♯​j∗​𝔛j_{\sharp}j^{*}\mathfrak{X} is simply 𝔛|U\mathfrak{X}|_{U} considered as a WW-scheme. If π|U\pi|_{U} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, then the map j♯​j∗​𝔛→Uj_{\sharp}j^{*}\mathfrak{X}\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence also. The top horizontal map is a cofibration, and so left properness of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-local model structure implies that 𝔛→i∗​𝔛Z\mathfrak{X}\to i_{*}\mathfrak{X}_{Z} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence as well. In essence, Theorem 3.1.1 shows that the additional control afforded by the section ss and the smoothness of ZZ allows us to identify the homotopy type of i∗​𝔛Zi_{*}\mathfrak{X}_{Z} more explicitly.

Remark 3.1.3.

If s:X→Bs:X\to B is the structure morphism of a smooth BB-scheme, and if ℰ\mathscr{E} is a finite rank locally free sheaf of 𝒪X\mathscr{O}_{X}-modules, then by a weak trivialization of ℰ\mathscr{E} we will mean a pair (ℰ0,φ)(\mathscr{E}_{0},\varphi) consisting of a finite rank locally free sheaf ℰ0\mathscr{E}_{0} of 𝒪B\mathscr{O}_{B}-modules and an isomorphism φ:ℰ→∼s∗​ℰ0\varphi:\mathscr{E}{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\scriptscriptstyle{\sim}}}}{{\;\rightarrow\;}}}s^{*}\mathscr{E}_{0}; we will say that ℰ\mathscr{E} is constant if it admits a weak trivialization. Extending [MV99, §3 Proposition 2.7(2)], if ℰ\mathscr{E} is a constant locally free sheaf of finite rank with a chosen weak trivialization (ℰ0,φ)(\mathscr{E}_{0},\varphi), then

Th(ℰ)≅Th(ℰ0)∧BX+.{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{E})\cong{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{E}_{0}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}_{B}X_{+}.

Indeed, this observation follows from that one by simply choosing an open cover of XX along which ℰ0\mathscr{E}_{0} is trivial.

While Theorem 3.1.1 does give some insight into the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of 𝔛\mathfrak{X}, it will be more useful with additional hypotheses in place. For example, we may use Theorem 3.1.1 to construct 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes via the following corollary.

Corollary 3.1.4.

Assume π:𝔛→W\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to W and Z→WZ\to W are as in Theorem 3.1.1. If the map 𝔛Z→Z\mathfrak{X}_{Z}\to Z is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, then 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Proof.

In the terminology of [Hoy17, Definition 3.17], the smooth pairs (W,Z)(W,Z) and (𝔛,𝔛Z)(\mathfrak{X},\mathfrak{X}_{Z}) are weakly excisive, so the assumption that 𝔛Z→Z\mathfrak{X}_{Z}\to Z is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence implies that the induced map Th⁡(𝒩Z/W)→Th⁡(𝒩𝔛Z/𝔛){\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{Z/W})\to{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{Z}/\mathfrak{X}}) is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence by properness of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-local model structure. ∎

3.2 A special case: smooth fibrations over affine spaces

We now reconsider Theorem 3.1.1 under more stringent hypotheses on ZZ and WW. In particular, if W=𝔸BnW={\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} and Z=0⊂𝔸BnZ=0\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B}, we may obtain a more precise description of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of 𝔛\mathfrak{X}. The following result establishes Theorem 2 from the introduction.

Theorem 3.2.1.

Assume 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is a BB-scheme, and π:𝔛→𝔸Bn\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B} is a smooth morphism admitting a section ss such that, if U:=π−1​(𝔸n∖0)U:=\pi^{-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0), then s|𝔸Bn∖0:𝔸Bn∖0→Us|_{{{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B}\smallsetminus 0}}:{{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B}\smallsetminus 0}\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. If 𝔛0:=π−1​(0)\mathfrak{X}_{0}:=\pi^{-1}(0), then there is a canonical (pointed) 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0,s⁡(0))∼(𝔛,s⁡(0)).{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge(\mathfrak{X}_{0},s(0))\sim(\mathfrak{X},s(0)).
Proof.

Since π\pi is smooth, it follows that 𝔛0\mathfrak{X}_{0} is a smooth BB-scheme. Moreover, since π\pi is flat, by choosing coordinates t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n}, i.e., an identification 𝔸Bn=Spec⁡𝒪B​[t1,…,tn]{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{B}=\operatorname{Spec}\mathscr{O}_{B}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}], it follows that t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n} is a regular sequence on 𝔛\mathfrak{X} and 𝔛0\mathfrak{X}_{0} is defined by the vanishing of t1,…,tnt_{1},\ldots,t_{n}. In particular, the normal sheaf 𝒩𝔛0/𝔛\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathfrak{X}} is equipped with a corresponding trivialization (we will call this the canonical trivialization in what follows). For notational clarity, we henceforth suppress BB from the notation (so, e.g., the zero sphere S0S^{0} is B+B_{+}, i.e., a disjoint union of two copies of BB).

Appealing to Theorem 3.1.1 and specializing the notation as necessary, we obtain the cofiber sequence of the form

Th⁡(𝒩0/𝔸n)⟶Th⁡(𝒩𝔛0/𝔛)⟶𝔛.{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{0/{\mathbb{A}}^{n}})\longrightarrow{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathfrak{X}})\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X}.

The canonical trivialization determines an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

Th⁡(𝒩𝔛0/𝔛)∼ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0)+{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathfrak{X}})\sim{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(\mathfrak{X}_{0})_{+}

(see [MV99, §3 Proposition 2.17] or Remark 3.1.3). The restriction of the canonical trivialization of 𝒩𝔛0/𝔛\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}/\mathfrak{X}} to 𝒩0/𝔸n\mathscr{N}_{0/{\mathbb{A}}^{n}} yields a corresponding trivialization of that normal sheaf and an identification

Th⁡(𝒩0/𝔸n)≅ℙ1∧n∧S0=ℙ1∧n.{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{0/{\mathbb{A}}^{n}})\cong{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge S^{0}={{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}.

Using the compatibility of these trivializations and the conclusions of the two preceding paragraphs, we see that:

  1. 1.

    There is a cofiber sequence of the form

    ℙ1∧n⟶ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0)+⟶𝔛.{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\longrightarrow{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(\mathfrak{X}_{0})_{+}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X}.
  2. 2.

    The left-hand morphism in the above cofiber sequence is the map ℙ1∧n=ℙ1∧n∧S0→ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0)+{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}={{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge S^{0}\to{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge(\mathfrak{X}_{0})_{+} corresponding to suspending the map S0→(𝔛0)+S^{0}\to(\mathfrak{X}_{0})_{+} given by sending the non-basepoint of S0S^{0} to s⁡(0)s(0), and consequently

  3. 3.

    The left-hand morphism in the above cofiber sequence is split.

Therefore, appealing to Proposition 1.2.3, there is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

ℙ1∧n∧(𝔛0)⟶∼𝔛,{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(\mathfrak{X}_{0}){\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\;\longrightarrow\;}}}\mathfrak{X},

with base-points as stated. ∎

As a variant of the above result, we may also analyze smooth morphisms 𝔛→𝔸B1\mathfrak{X}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} that have multiple degenerate fibers.

Theorem 3.2.2.

Assume 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is a BB-scheme, and π:𝔛→𝔸B1\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} is a smooth morphism admitting a section ss. Assume there exists a closed immersion of BB-schemes i:Z↪𝔸B1i:Z\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} with open complement U⊂𝔸B1U\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} having the following properties:

  1. 1.

    The immersion ii is defined by a monic polynomial g∈𝒪B​[t]g\in\mathscr{O}_{B}[t] that factors as a product of linear factors with roots in BB.

  2. 2.

    There exists a closed subscheme Z~=B⊔⋯⊔B\tilde{Z}=B\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B having the same open complement as ZZ such that Z~\tilde{Z} is smooth over BB.

  3. 3.

    The morphism π:π−1​(U)→U\pi:\pi^{-1}(U)\to U is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Write bib_{i}, i=1,⋯,ri=1,\cdots,r for the inclusion of the ii-th factor of BB in Z~\tilde{Z}, 𝔛bi\mathfrak{X}_{b_{i}} for the base-change of π\pi along the morphism B→𝔸B1B\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} determined by bib_{i}, and point 𝔛bi\mathfrak{X}_{b_{i}} by xix_{i}, obtained from bib_{i} and ss. In that case, there is a pointed 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

ℙ1∧(⋁i=1r𝔛bi)∼𝔛,{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\wedge(\bigvee_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{X}_{b_{i}})\sim\mathfrak{X},

where 𝔛\mathfrak{X} is pointed by any base-point xix_{i}.

Remark 3.2.3.

Before getting to the proof, let us observe that conditions in the theorem are easy to check when BB is an integral affine scheme. Indeed, in that case, since gg is a product of linear factors, we can find a separable polynomial g~\tilde{g} that divides gg. The smoothness condition is equivalent to the assertion that the discriminant disc⁡(g~)\operatorname{disc}(\tilde{g}) is a unit in each residue field at a closed point.

Proof.

Write 𝔛Z~\mathfrak{X}_{\tilde{Z}} for the fiber product of Z~\tilde{Z} and 𝔛\mathfrak{X} over 𝔸Z1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{Z}; note that the base-change of π\pi along Z~→Z\tilde{Z}\to Z is a smooth morphism, so the fibers 𝔛bi\mathfrak{X}_{b_{i}} corresponding to the components of Z~\tilde{Z} are all smooth schemes. Choose base-points as in the statement of the theorem.

In that case, we may appeal to Theorem 3.1.1. In particular, there is a cofiber sequence of the form

Th⁡(𝒩Z~/𝔸B1)⟶Th⁡(𝒩𝔛Z~/𝔛Z)⟶𝔛.{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{\tilde{Z}/{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B}})\longrightarrow{\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{\mathfrak{X}_{\tilde{Z}}/\mathfrak{X}_{Z}})\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X}.

Note that Z~\tilde{Z} is cut out by a separable polynomial g~\tilde{g} that divides gg. This element also defines a principal divisor on 𝔛\mathfrak{X} that cuts out 𝔛Z~\mathfrak{X}_{\tilde{Z}}. It follows that the normal sheaf to each embedding is equipped with a trivialization, and these trivializations are compatible. Therefore, the above cofiber sequence reads:

ℙ1∧Z~+⟶ℙ1∧(𝔛Z~)+⟶𝔛.{\mathbb{P}}^{1}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}\tilde{Z}_{+}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{1}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(\mathfrak{X}_{\tilde{Z}})_{+}\longrightarrow\mathfrak{X}.

Now, if (𝒴i,yi)(\mathscr{Y}_{i},y_{i}) is a finite collection of pointed spaces, for any j∈Ij\in I, we may write

(⊔i∈I𝒴i)+=(𝒴j)+∨(⊔i∈I∖{j}𝒴i)+.(\sqcup_{i\in I}\mathscr{Y}_{i})_{+}=(\mathscr{Y}_{j})_{+}\vee(\sqcup_{i\in I\smallsetminus\{j\}}\mathscr{Y}_{i})_{+}.

Using this observation, the result follows by repeated appeal to Proposition 1.2.3. ∎

Example 3.2.4.

Assume that B=Spec⁡kB=\operatorname{Spec}k for some base ring kk and let (X,∗)⊂𝔸kn+1(X,\ast)\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n+1}_{k} is a pointed smooth hypersurface defined by the vanishing of a polynomial f∈k⁡[z1,…,zn+1]f\in k[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n+1}] and a kk-point ∗\ast of XX. Let i:Z↪𝔸k1i:Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k} be a hypersurface defined by a polynomial g=∏i=1r(t−ai)big=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(t-a_{i})^{b_{i}}, ai∈ka_{i}\in k, bi∈ℤ>0b_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} such that the hypersurface Z~\tilde{Z} defined by the polynomial g~=∏i=1r(t−ai)\tilde{g}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(t-a_{i}) is smooth over kk.

Then the hypersurface 𝔛g⊂𝔸kn+3\mathfrak{X}_{g}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n+3}_{k} defined by the equation f−g​x=0f-gx=0 is smooth over kk and there is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence

𝔛g∼(∨i=1rℙ1)∧(X,∗).\mathfrak{X}_{g}\sim(\vee_{i=1}^{r}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(X,\ast).

Indeed, let π:𝔛g→𝔸k1\pi:\mathfrak{X}_{g}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} be the morphism induced by the projection onto the xx-variable. The ring homomorphism OPENk⁡[t,z1,…,zn+1,x])→k⁡[t,x]k[t,z_{1},\ldots,z_{n+1},x])\to k[t,x] factors through a ring homomorphism k⁡[𝔛g]→k⁡[t,x]k[\mathfrak{X}_{g}]\to k[t,x] which yields a section of π\pi. The fibers of π:𝔛g→𝔸k1\pi:\mathfrak{X}_{g}\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k} over the points in 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} where gg vanishes are isomorphic to the total spaces of line bundles over XX (the normal bundles to the embedding of the given component). In particular, each such fiber is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to XX. The claimed 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence thus follows from Theorem 3.2.2, together with the identification ℙ1∧(∨i=1r(X,x))∼(∨i=1rℙ1)∧(X,x){\mathbb{P}}^{1}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(\vee_{i=1}^{r}(X,x))\sim(\vee_{i=1}^{r}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(X,x).

Remark 3.2.5.

For this remark, we work over the complex numbers. If f⁡(𝐱)f({\bf x}) and g⁡(𝐲)g({\bf y}) are polynomials in mm and nn variables, then we write f⊕gf\oplus g for the polynomial f⁡(𝐱)+g⁡(𝐲)f({\bf x})+g({\bf y}) in n+mn+m-variables. The classical “global” Thom–Sebastiani theorem [N9́1, Theorem 2.4] states that the homotopy type of general fibers of f⊕gf\oplus g is the join of the homotopy types of the general fiber of ff and the general fiber of gg. A straightforward analog of this theorem in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory cannot be true because the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of the fibers of ff can vary rather wildly. Example 3.2.4 provides one version of such a theorem in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory. The general fiber of g​tgt is Spec⁡k⁡[x,1g]=𝔸k1∖{x1,…,xr}⊂𝔸k1\operatorname{Spec}k[x,\frac{1}{g}]={\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}\smallsetminus\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} and the join of 𝔸k1∖{x1,…,xr}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}\smallsetminus\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\} and (X,x)(X,x) coincides with the wedge sum of a number of copies of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} with (X,x)(X,x) by appeal to the purity isomorphism.

4 Examples and applications

In this section, we put the results of the preceding sections together and study applications. For example, Section 4.1 shows that iterated ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspensions of smooth schemes admit smooth models in a rather great generality. The remainder of the section is concerned with building other schemes with controlled 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy types.

4.1 Deformation spaces model suspensions

Suppose (X,x)(X,x) is a pointed smooth kk-scheme. If YY is a smooth kk-scheme and i:X↪Yi:X\hookrightarrow Y is a closed immersion, we will point YY by i⁡(x)i(x). If D⁡(X,Y){\mathrm{D}}(X,Y) is the deformation space of ii (see Example 2.1.3), then there is a canonical closed immersion X↪NX/Y↪D⁡(X,Y)X\hookrightarrow{N}_{X/Y}\hookrightarrow{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y), where NX/Y{N}_{X/Y} is the total space of the normal sheaf 𝒩X/Y\mathscr{N}_{X/Y}, and we point D⁡(X,Y){\mathrm{D}}(X,Y) by the image of xx under this composite morphism. Note that the choice of base-point determines a section of the morphism D⁡(X,Y)→𝔸1{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. With this convention, we may now state the following result.

Theorem 4.1.1.

Assume BB is a base scheme and (X,x)(X,x) is a pointed smooth BB-scheme. If there exists an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth BB-scheme YY and a (pointed) closed immersion X↪YX\hookrightarrow Y, then there is a pointed 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence:

Σℙ1​X⟶D⁡(X,Y).\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X\longrightarrow{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y).
Proof.

By appeal to Corollary 2.2.3, we see that the projection D⁡(X,Y)→𝔸B1{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{B} satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.2.1 (the section arises from the base-point). In that case, we conclude that Σℙ1​D​(X,Y)0∼D⁡(X,Y)\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)_{0}\sim{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y), where D​(X,Y)0{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)_{0} is the scheme-theoretic fiber of the projection over 00. However, D​(X,Y)0{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)_{0} is the total space of the normal bundle to the embedding X↪YX\hookrightarrow Y, and therefore the projection map D​(X,Y)0→X{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)_{0}\to X is a (pointed) 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Thus, we conclude that Σℙ1​D​(X,Y)0→Σℙ1​X\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}{\mathrm{D}}(X,Y)_{0}\to\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X is a (pointed) 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence as well. ∎

The following result gives a rather general condition when the hypotheses of the preceding theorem are satisfied.

Proposition 4.1.2.

If BB is a qcqs base scheme, and XX is a finitely presented smooth affine BB-scheme, then there exists a finitely presented smooth 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible BB-scheme YY and a closed immersion of BB-schemes X→YX\to Y.

Proof.

In light of the finite presentation hypotheses, there exists a Noetherian scheme B0B_{0}, a morphism B→B0B\to B_{0} and a finitely-presented affine B0B_{0}-scheme X0X_{0} such that X=X0×B0BX=X_{0}\times_{B_{0}}B [Sta19, Tag 01Z6] and the structure morphism X0→B0X_{0}\to B_{0} may also be assumed affine. In that case, the result is classical: covering B0B_{0} by affines, we may glue together embeddings corresponding to local generators to obtain a vector bundle over B0B_{0} into which X0X_{0} embeds (this is evidently a finitely presented BB-scheme). The base-change of this vector bundle to BB is again a vector bundle, and thus XX comes equipped with a closed immersion into this vector bundle. ∎

We can also extend Theorem 4.1.1 to the situation where a space admits an embedding into an affine space up to homotopy. To that end, write SmBaff\mathrm{Sm}^{\operatorname{aff}}_{B} for the full subcategory of SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B} consisting of schemes that are affine in the absolute sense.

Definition 4.1.3.

A Jouanolou device for X∈SmBX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{B} consists of a pair (X~,φ)(\tilde{X},\varphi) where X~∈SmBaff\tilde{X}\in\mathrm{Sm}_{B}^{\operatorname{aff}} and φ:X~→X\varphi:\tilde{X}\to X is a morphism making X~\tilde{X} into a torsor under a vector bundle over XX.

Jouanolou observed [Jou73, Lemme 1.5] that quasi-projective schemes always possess affine vector bundle torsors; Thomason extended this fact, and we recall these results here.

Proposition 4.1.4 (Jouanolou–Thomason homotopy lemma).

Suppose BB is a qcqs base scheme.

  1. 1.

    If X∈SmBX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{B} admits an ample family of line bundles, then XX admits a Jouanolou device.

  2. 2.

    If BB is furthermore quasi-compact and regular, and X∈SmBX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{B} has affine diagonal and is quasi-compact over BB, then XX admits a Jouanolou device.

Proof.

The first assertion is a restatement of [Wei89, Proposition 4.4] in our context. For the second assertion, since XX has an affine diagonal, the structure morphism is quasi-separated. Since the structure morphism is quasi-compact by assumption, it follows that XX is finitely presented over BB.

Since XX is finitely presented and smooth over BB, which is regular, we claim that XX is regular. To see this, first, observe that XX is automatically quasi-compact. To check its local rings are regular, we may reduce to the affine case, so B=Spec⁡RB=\operatorname{Spec}R is affine and X=Spec⁡SX=\operatorname{Spec}S, so φ:R→S\varphi:R\to S is a smooth ring map with AA regular. In particular, this means that SS is a Noetherian RR-algebra. Moreover, smoothness implies φ\varphi is a flat ring map with regular fibers. Let 𝔮⊂S{\mathfrak{q}}\subset S be a prime ideal, and let 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} be its pre-image in RR. Choose a regular sequence f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} in R𝔭R_{{\mathfrak{p}}} that generates 𝔭​R𝔭{\mathfrak{p}}R_{{\mathfrak{p}}}. Since R→SR\to S is flat the image of f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} in SS is again a regular sequence. Moreover, S𝔭/(φ⁡(f1),…,φ⁡(fn))S_{{\mathfrak{p}}}/(\varphi(f_{1}),\ldots,\varphi(f_{n})) is a fiber of φ\varphi hence regular. It follows that S𝔭S_{{\mathfrak{p}}} is regular, and thus so is S𝔮S_{{\mathfrak{q}}}.

Finally, since XX is regular, it is automatically locally factorial by the Auslander–Buchsbaum theorem [Sta19, Tag 0AG0] (in particular normal). In that case, appeal to [BS03, Proposition 1.3] implies that XX carries an ample family of line bundles. Then, the second point follows from the first. ∎

Example 4.1.5.

Some separation hypothesis is necessary for Proposition 4.1.4 to guarantee the existence of a Jouanolou device. If n≥1n\geq 1, then write 𝔸2⋅0n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{2\cdot 0} for the quasi-separated kk-scheme given by the affine nn-space with a doubled origin; while this scheme fails to be separated, it has affine diagonal if and only if n=1n=1.

The scheme 𝔸2⋅01{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{2\cdot 0} has a Jouanolou device; in fact, a “standard” choice of a Jouanolou device is the hypersurface given by x​y=z⁡(1+z)xy=z(1+z) in 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{k}. In more detail, consider the inclusion of 𝔾m⊂SL2{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\subset\operatorname{SL}_{2} as diagonal matrices with determinant 11. An explicit computation with invariants identifies the quotient SL2/𝔾m\operatorname{SL}_{2}/{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} with the hypersurface in 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3} defined by the equation x​y=z⁡(1+z)xy=z(1+z). On the other hand, consider the map SL2→𝔸2∖0\operatorname{SL}_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0 corresponding to projection onto the first column; this map is 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}-equivariant for the action of 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} on 𝔸2∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0 given by t⋅(x,y)=(t​x,t−1​y)t\cdot(x,y)=(tx,t^{-1}y), but is also a 𝔾a{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}{}-torsor. The geometric quotient of 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} acting on 𝔸2∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0 exists as a smooth scheme and is identified with 𝔸2⋅01{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{2\cdot 0} by explicit computation: if we cover 𝔸2∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0 with the two open sets 𝔸2∖{x=0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{x=0\} and 𝔸2∖{y=0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{y=0\}, then the function x​yxy is invariant and yields identifications 𝔸2∖{x=0}/𝔾m≅𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{x=0\}/{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and 𝔸2∖0∖y=0/𝔾m≅𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0\smallsetminus{y=0}/{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. It follows that the 𝔾a{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}{}-torsor SL2→𝔸2∖0\operatorname{SL}_{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0 descends to a 𝔾a{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}{}-torsor SL2/𝔾m→𝔸2⋅01\operatorname{SL}_{2}/{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{2\cdot 0} with the formulas given above.

By contrast, when n>1n>1, the scheme 𝔸2⋅0n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{2\cdot 0} has strictly quasi-affine diagonal11 1 The condition of having quasi-affine diagonal is equivalent to quasi-separateness because the diagonal morphism of a scheme is always an immersion [Sta19, Tag 01KJ] and quasi-compact immersions are quasi-affine [Sta19, Tag 02JR]. and does not have a Jouanolou device; this is, of course, related to Thomason’s observation that such schemes do not possess the resolution property [TT90, Exercise 8.6]. Indeed, take k=ℤk={\mathbb{Z}} and suppose π:X→𝔸2⋅0n\pi:X\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{2\cdot 0} is a torsor under a vector bundle. Since a torsor under a vector bundle on an affine scheme admits a section, hence is a vector bundle, and vector bundles on 𝔸ℤn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}} are trivial by the Quillen–Suslin theorem, the restriction of π\pi over either copy of 𝔸ℤn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}} is isomorphic to a trivial bundle. On the other hand, since the inclusion 𝔸ℤn∖0→𝔸ℤn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}\smallsetminus 0\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}} has complement of codimension ≥2\geq 2, and 𝔸ℤn∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}\smallsetminus 0 is normal, any isomorphism between the two restrictions π\pi over 𝔸ℤn∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}\smallsetminus 0 extends over 𝔸ℤn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}. Thus, one obtains a global isomorphism of XX with a product 𝔸ℤn×𝔸2⋅0n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{2\cdot 0}, in particular, XX is not affine.

With the Jouanolou–Thomason homotopy lemma in hand, we can extend Theorem 4.1.1 to the situation of schemes that may be embedded in an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible scheme up to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy.

Corollary 4.1.6.

Assume BB is a regular affine base scheme.

  1. 1.

    If (X,x)(X,x) is a quasi-compact smooth BB-scheme with affine diagonal, then for any integer i≥0i\geq 0, the iterated ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension Σℙ1i​X\Sigma^{i}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X has the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of a smooth BB-scheme as well.

  2. 2.

    If (X,x)(X,x) is furthermore affine, then Σℙ1i​X\Sigma^{i}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X admits a smooth affine model as well.

Proof.

Under the assumptions on BB, XX satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition 4.1.4. In particular, there exists a smooth BB-scheme X~\tilde{X} and vector bundle torsor X~→X\tilde{X}\to X with affine total space X~\tilde{X}. The morphism X~→X\tilde{X}\to X is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Since (X,x)(X,x) is pointed, we have a morphism x:Spec⁡B→Xx:\operatorname{Spec}B\to X. If we base-change X~\tilde{X} along xx, we obtain an affine vector bundle torsor B~→B\tilde{B}\to B. Since BB is affine by assumption, B~→B\tilde{B}\to B is isomorphic to a vector bundle over BB; fix such an isomorphism, and define a morphism x~:B→B~\tilde{x}:B\to\tilde{B} to be the image of the zero section under the isomorphism. Composing this section with the canonical morphism B~→X~\tilde{B}\to\tilde{X} from the fiber product, we see that (X~,x~)→(X,x)(\tilde{X},\tilde{x})\to(X,x) is a pointed 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Therefore, without loss of generality, we may replace (X,x)(X,x) by (X~,x~)(\tilde{X},\tilde{x}) and assume that XX is affine.

In that case, fix a closed embedding ι:X↪Y\iota:X\hookrightarrow Y for YY some 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth BB-scheme; such an embedding exists by appeal to Proposition 4.1.2. Granted this observation, the first point follows immediately by inductive appeal to Theorem 4.1.1. Note also that if YY is a smooth affine BB-scheme, then the deformation space D⁡(X,Y){\mathrm{D}}(X,Y) is automatically a smooth affine BB-scheme as well, so the second point follows also. ∎

This following observation generalizes [ADF17, Theorem 2].

Corollary 4.1.7.

For every integer n≥0n\geq 0, ℙ1∧n{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n} and 𝔾m∧ℙ1∧n{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n} have the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of smooth separated ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-schemes.

Proof.

The ring homomorphism ℤ⁡[t]→ℤ⁡[t]/(t⁡(1−t)){\mathbb{Z}}[t]\to{\mathbb{Z}}[t]/(t(1-t)) defines a closed immersion of smooth schemes Sℤ0→𝔸ℤ1S^{0}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}. Likewise, the ring homomorphism ℤ⁡[t1,t2]↦ℤ⁡[t1,t2]/(t1​t2−1){\mathbb{Z}}[t_{1},t_{2}]\mapsto{\mathbb{Z}}[t_{1},t_{2}]/(t_{1}t_{2}-1) defines a closed immersion of smooth schemes 𝔾m→𝔸ℤ2{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{{\mathbb{Z}}}. The assertion then follows from Corollary 4.1.6. ∎

Remark 4.1.8.

Note that no separation hypothesis is imposed on objects of SmB\mathrm{Sm}_{B} in the construction of H⁡(B)\mathrm{H}({B}). If we do not restrict our attention to smooth separated BB-schemes, affine nn-space with doubled origin provides a model for ℙ1∧n{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n} as a smooth BB-scheme. Indeed, the homotopy colimit of the diagram

𝔸n⟵𝔸n∖0⟶𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\longleftarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0\longrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}

coincides with the homotopy pushout of 𝔸n∖0→𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n} (contract the 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} on the left to a point), i.e., Th⁡(𝒩0/𝔸n){\operatorname{Th}}(\mathscr{N}_{0/{\mathbb{A}}^{n}}), which becomes 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to ℙ1∧n{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n} after fixing a basis of the tangent space at 00. More generally, the affine space nn-space with mm-fold origin provides a model for ⋁m−1ℙ1∧n\bigvee^{m-1}{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}.

Question 4.1.9.

Fix an infinite field kk, and a smooth affine kk-scheme XX of dimension dd. If i>0i>0 is an integer, what is the minimum dimension of a smooth affine model of Σℙ1i​X\Sigma^{i}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X?

Remark 4.1.10.

If kk is an infinite field, and XX is a smooth affine kk-scheme of dimension dd, then it is well-known that XX can be embedded as a closed subscheme of 𝔸2​d+1{\mathbb{A}}^{2d+1} and that this bound is optimal [BMS89, Theorem 5.8]. Given the choice of one such closed embedding X↪𝔸2​d+1X\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2d+1}, Theorem 4.1.1 provides a model D⁡(X,𝔸2​d+1){\mathrm{D}}(X,{\mathbb{A}}^{2d+1}) of Σℙ1​X\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X of dimension 2​d+22d+2.

4.2 Highly 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-connected hypersurfaces

In this section, we analyze a variation of a construction due to Danielewski [Dan88, Fie94] to produce hypersurfaces that are “highly 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected”. Indeed, up to change of variables, Danielewski studied the varieties xn​y=z⁡(1−z)x^{n}y=z(1-z) as nn varies. In the context of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, these varieties are all Jouanolou devices for the affine line with doubled origin 𝔸2⋅01{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{2\cdot 0} discussed previously in Example 4.1.5, and Danielewski was interested in analyzing their isomorphism types (these varieties are all stably isomorphic). The second author considered a significant generalization of the Danielewski construction in [Dub05a, Dub07] and the version we analyze here can be viewed as axiomatizing some of the key properties considered in those papers.

A family of generic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences

Construction 4.2.1.

Suppose kk is a base ring. Assume Y⊂𝔸knY\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is defined by a finitely generated ideal I=(f1,…,fr)⊂k⁡[x1,…,xn]I=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{r})\subset k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Fix an integer ss, and suppose a1,…,as∈k⁡[x1,…,xn]a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}\in k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] are polynomials. For 𝐚=(a1,…,as){\bf a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}) we define

XI,𝐚={∑itifi=∏j=1s(z−aj)}⊂𝔸kn+r+1.X_{I,{\bf a}}=\{\sum_{i}t_{i}f_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{s}(z-a_{j})\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n+r+1}_{k}.

Let π:XI,𝐚→𝔸kn\pi:X_{I,{\bf a}}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{n}_{k} be the morphism defined by the inclusion of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] into the coordinate ring of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}}.

Proposition 4.2.2.

In the setting of Construction 4.2.1, assume that XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} is flat over kk and that the functions {fi}i=1,…,r,{aj}j=1,…,s\{f_{i}\}_{i=1,\ldots,r},\{a_{j}\}_{j=1,\ldots,s} are not zero-divisors. Then the following statements hold about the morphism π:XI,𝐚→𝔸kn\pi:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}.

  1. 1.

    The restriction of π\pi to 𝔸kn∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y is a Zariski locally trivial smooth morphism with affine space fibers.

  2. 2.

    The morphism π\pi admits a section, and if we set Y′=Spec⁡k⁡[x1,…,xn,z]/(∏i=1s(z−ai),I)Y^{\prime}=\operatorname{Spec}k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},z]/(\prod_{i=1}^{s}(z-a_{i}),I), the base-change of π\pi along the inclusion Y↪𝔸knY\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} factors as

    𝔸Y′n⟶Y′⟶Y.{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{Y^{\prime}}\longrightarrow Y^{\prime}\longrightarrow Y.
  3. 3.

    The morphism π\pi is finitely presented and faithfully flat.

  4. 4.

    The morphism π\pi is smooth if and only if Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y is étale.

  5. 5.

    If the morphism π\pi is smooth, then it factors through a smooth morphism π′:XI,𝐚→𝔸s​Yn\pi^{\prime}:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY} where the target is the non-separated scheme obtained by gluing ss copies of 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} with the identity map along 𝔸kn∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y.

Proof.

Put S=k⁡[x1,…,xn,t1,…,tr,z]S=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},t_{1},\ldots,t_{r},z], f=∑iti​fi−∏j(z−aj)∈Sf=\sum_{i}t_{i}f_{i}-\prod_{j}(z-a_{j})\in S and R=S/(f)R=S/(f).

1. By assumption, fif_{i} is not a zero-divisor. Inverting any fif_{i} yields an isomorphism

S⁡[fi−1]≅k⁡[x1,…,xn,fi−1]​[t1,…,t^i,…,tr,z],S[f_{i}^{-1}]\cong k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},f_{i}^{-1}][t_{1},\ldots,\hat{t}_{i},\ldots,t_{r},z],

showing that the restriction of π\pi to the principal open set D⁡(fi)D(f_{i}) of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} is thus isomorphic to the trivial 𝔸r\mathbb{A}^{r}-bundle over the principal open set D⁡(fi)D(f_{i}) of 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n}. This provides an explicit local trivialization of π\pi over 𝔸kn∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y.

2. Fix an integer j∈{1,…,s}j\in\{1,\ldots,s\} and observe that sending ti,i=1,…,rt_{i},i=1,\ldots,r to 00 and setting z=ajz=a_{j} defines a section of π\pi. The factor ring S′=k⁡[x1,…,xn,t1,…,tr,z]/(∏i=1sz−ai,I)S^{\prime}=k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},t_{1},\ldots,t_{r},z]/(\prod_{i=1}^{s}z-a_{i},I) of SS defines the closed subscheme scheme Y′⊂XI,𝐚Y^{\prime}\subset X_{I,{\bf a}}. By definition, we have a commutative square of the form

where the horizontal morphisms are closed immersions.The restriction of the section π\pi to YY yields a section Y→Y′Y\to Y^{\prime}. The base-change of π\pi along YY factors as

(4.2.1) 𝔸Y′n⟶Y′⟶Y,{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{Y^{\prime}}\longrightarrow Y^{\prime}\longrightarrow Y,

where 𝔸Y′n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{Y^{\prime}} is the spectrum of the polynomial ring in the variables t1,…,trt_{1},\ldots,t_{r} over S′S^{\prime}.

3. That π\pi is surjective is immediate because it admits a section. That π\pi has finite presentation is immediate from the definitions. Thus, it remains to check that π\pi is flat. Since zz and the tit_{i} are not zero-divisors and the fif_{i} and aia_{i} are not zero-divisors by assumption, it follows that f=∑ifi​ti−∏i=1s(z−ai)f=\sum_{i}f_{i}t_{i}-\prod_{i=1}^{s}(z-a_{i}) is not a zero-divisor in RR. By assumption XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} is flat over kk, which means that SS is a flat kk-module. Let AA be the localization of k⁡[x1,…,xn]k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] at a prime ideal 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}} and let BB be the localization of RR at a prime ideal 𝔮\mathfrak{q} lying above 𝔭{\mathfrak{p}}. Note that by construction, BB is essentially finitely presented over AA, and A→BA\to B is a flat ring map. Let mm be the maximal ideal of AA. Since ff is not a zero-divisor in RR, its image in B/𝔪​BB/{\mathfrak{m}}B is not a zero-divisor. By appeal to [Sta19, Tag 046Z], we conclude that B/(f)B/(f) is flat over AA. Since AA and BB were arbitrary, it follows that π\pi is flat.

4. Since π\pi is flat and of finite presentation by assumption, to check it is smooth, it suffices to check that its fibers are smooth. This statement is immediate over points in 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} that are contained in the complement of YY, so it suffices to check smoothness over points of YY. To this end, consider the factorization of π\pi from (4.2.1). If Y′Y^{\prime} is étale over YY, then this composite is evidently smooth, which shows that π\pi is smooth. Conversely, if π\pi is smooth, then the composite morphism in (4.2.1) is smooth as well. The first morphism in that factorization is always smooth and surjective. The morphism Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y is evidently of finite presentation. Therefore, [Sta19, Tag 02K5] shows that Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y must also be smooth. In that case, considerations of relative dimension imply that Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y must also have relative dimension 00, in which case it is automatically étale.

5. Under the assumption that π\pi is smooth, Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y is étale by the preceding point. We build the required factorization by gluing. The statement is tautological if s=1s=1, so assume s≥2s\geq 2. In that case, define EjE_{j} to be the closed subscheme of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} defined by f1=⋯=fr=∏i≠j(z−ai)=0f_{1}=\cdots=f_{r}=\prod_{i\neq j}(z-a_{i})=0. Set Xj=XI,𝐚∖EjX_{j}=X_{I,{\bf a}}\smallsetminus E_{j}. Note that {Xj}j=1,…,s\{X_{j}\}_{j=1,\ldots,s} forms an open cover of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}}. The restriction of π\pi to XjX_{j} defines a smooth morphism πj:Xj→𝔸kn\pi_{j}:X_{j}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}. For any j≠j′j\neq j^{\prime}, the intersection Xj∩Xj′X_{j}\cap X_{j^{\prime}} is π−1​(𝔸kn∖Y)\pi^{-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y), so the restrictions of πj\pi_{j} and πj′\pi_{j^{\prime}} to Xj∩Xj′X_{j}\cap X_{j^{\prime}} coincide with the restriction of π\pi to 𝔸kn∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y. It follows that the morphisms πj\pi_{j} glue to yield the morphism π′:XI,𝐚⟶𝔸s​Yn,\pi^{\prime}:X_{I,{\bf a}}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY}, which is smooth by construction. ∎

In the case where II is a principal ideal, the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of the varieties from Proposition 4.2.2 is relatively straightforward to identify.

Lemma 4.2.3.

Assume kk is a normal Noetherian domain such that P​i​c​(k)=0Pic(k)=0 (e.g., kk is a UFD). Consider the scheme XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} from Proposition 4.2.2, where I=(f)I=(f) is principal and assume that s≥2s\geq 2. Let Xj:=XI,𝐚∖EjX_{j}:=X_{I,{\bf a}}\smallsetminus E_{j}, where EjE_{j} is the closed subscheme defined by the ideal (I,∏i≠j(z−ai))(I,\prod_{i\neq j}(z-a_{i})). Then the following hold:

  1. 1.

    The scheme XjX_{j} is isomorphic to 𝔸kn+1{\mathbb{A}}^{n+1}_{k}.

  2. 2.

    If the morphism π:XI,𝐚→𝔸kn\pi:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is smooth, then the projection morphism π′:XI,𝐚→𝔸s​Yn\pi^{\prime}:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY} is a Jouanolou device (in particular an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence).

  3. 3.

    If 𝔸n∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus Y has a kk-point, then there is a (pointed) 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence XI,𝐚∼⋁i=1s−1(Σ​𝔸n∖Y)X_{I,{\bf a}}\sim\bigvee_{i=1}^{s-1}(\Sigma{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus Y). If Yr​e​dY_{red} is furthermore smooth over Spec⁡k\operatorname{Spec}k, then XI,𝐚∼(∨i=1s−1ℙ1)∧(Yr​e​d)+X_{I,{\bf a}}\sim(\vee_{i=1}^{s-1}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(Y_{red})_{+}.

Proof.

We first note that under our assumptions, every Zariski locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundler over 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is globally trivial. Indeed, recall that the automorphism group A​u​t​(𝔸k1)Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}) is the affine group 𝔾mk⋉𝔾ak{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}_{k}\ltimes{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}{}_{k}. Since 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is affine, HZar1​(𝔸kn,𝔾a)=0H^{1}_{\operatorname{Zar}}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k},{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}{})=0 and since kk is Noetherian and normal, homotopy invariance of Picard groups [BM67, Corollary 5.10] guarantees that HZar1​(𝔸kn,𝔾m)=P​i​c​(𝔸kn)=P​i​c​(Spec⁡k)H^{1}_{\operatorname{Zar}}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k},{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}})=Pic({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k})=Pic(\operatorname{Spec}k) which is trivial by assumption. Therefore, the long exact sequence in non-abelian cohomology [Gir71, Proposition III.3.3.1] attached to the short exact sequence of sheaves of groups

1⟶𝔾a,k⟶A​u​t​(𝔸k1)⟶𝔾mk⟶11\longrightarrow\mathbb{G}_{a,k}\longrightarrow Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k})\longrightarrow{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}_{k}\longrightarrow 1

allows us to conclude that HZar1​(𝔸kn,A​u​t​(𝔸k1))H^{1}_{\operatorname{Zar}}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k},Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k})) is also trivial.

1. By the observation above, it suffices to show that πj\pi_{j} is a Zariski locally trivial 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}-bundle. By construction, the morphism πj:Xj→𝔸kn\pi_{j}:X_{j}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a Zariski locally trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle over 𝔸n∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus Y. Likewise, the morphism πj−1​(Y)→Y\pi_{j}^{-1}(Y)\to Y is a trivial 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-bundle, by the factorization from Proposition 4.2.2. All fibers of π\pi are thus isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}. Since 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a normal Noetherian scheme, [KW85, Theorem] implies that π\pi is a Zariski locally trivial 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}-bundle.

2. The fact that π′\pi^{\prime} is a torsor under a line bundle follows immediately from gluing and the fact that the morphism πj:Xj→𝔸kn\pi_{j}:X_{j}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a trivial 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}-bundle by the preceding point.

3. This follows from the previous point and a computation of the homotopy colimit of the diagram consisting of ss maps from 𝔸n∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus Y to ∗\ast. Indeed, the homotopy colimit of ss-maps from any (pointed) scheme WW to ∗\ast is a wedge sum of s−1s-1 copies of Σ​W\Sigma W. Then, the cofiber sequence 𝔸kn∖Y→𝔸kn→𝔸kn/(𝔸kn∖Y){\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}/({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y) and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility of 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} shows that 𝔸kn/(𝔸kn∖Y)∼Σ​𝔸kn∖Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}/({\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y)\sim\Sigma{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y. If Yr​e​dY_{red} is smooth, then Yr​e​d→𝔸knY_{red}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a regular immersion, and the normal bundle to this embedding has an explicit trivialization given by ff. In that case, homotopy purity implies that Σ​𝔸kn∖Y≅ℙ1∧(Yr​e​d)+\Sigma{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}\smallsetminus Y\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{1}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(Y_{red})_{+}. ∎

Remark 4.2.4.

Assuming Yr​e​dY_{red} is smooth, Lemma 4.2.3 gives complete control of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}}. Thus, for example, if ff and f′f^{\prime} define smooth plane curves in 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} whose Picard groups are non-isomorphic and a0=0,a1=1a_{0}=0,a_{1}=1, then the affine surfaces

X(f),𝐚={ft−z(z−1)=0}andX(f′),𝐚={f′t−z(z−1)=0}X_{(f),{\bf a}}=\{ft-z(z-1)=0\}\quad\textrm{and}\;\;\;\;\;\;\;X_{(f^{\prime}),{\bf a}}=\{f^{\prime}t-z(z-1)=0\}

are not isomorphic. Note, however, that the isomorphism type of XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} does depend in general on the scheme structure of YY as well. For example, take a0=0,a1=1a_{0}=0,a_{1}=1, and let f⊂𝔸k1f\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} be given by xrx^{r}. In that case, XI,𝐚X_{I,{\bf a}} is the Danielewski hypersurface xr​t=z⁡(z−1)x^{r}t=z(z-1) whose isomorphism type is known to be determined by rr [Cra06, Dan88, Dub05a, Fie94].

Example 4.2.5.

Suppose B=Spec⁡kB=\operatorname{Spec}k where kk is an integral domain. Assume P⁡(z)=∏i=1s(z−ai)P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{s}(z-a_{i}) with the aia_{i} pairwise distinct elements of kk and furthermore assume that disc⁡(P)\operatorname{disc}(P) is a unit in every residue field at a maximal ideal of kk. Given a vector 𝐦=(m1,…,mn){\bf m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{n}), mi∈ℤ>0m_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{>0}, consider the scheme

Q𝐦,P:={∑i=1nximiti=P(z)}.Q_{{\bf m},P}:=\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{m_{i}}t_{i}=P(z)\}.

In the setting of Construction 4.2.1, we have Q𝐦,P=XI,𝐚Q_{{\bf m},P}=X_{I,{\bf a}} for I=(x1m1,…,xnmn)I=(x_{1}^{m_{1}},\ldots,x_{n}^{m_{n}}) and 𝐚=(a1,…,as)\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{s}). The condition on P⁡(z)P(z) guarantees that Spec⁡k⁡[z]/P\operatorname{Spec}k[z]/P is smooth over Spec⁡k\operatorname{Spec}k, hence that Q𝐦,PQ_{{\bf m},P} is a smooth kk-scheme. Since the corresponding scheme Yr​e​dY_{red} is simply the origin in 𝔸kn\mathbb{A}^{n}_{k}, we obtain by Remark 4.3.2 that

Q𝐦,P∼(∨i=1s−1ℙ1∧c)∧(Yr​e​d)+∼(ℙ1∧n)∨d​e​g​P−1.Q_{{\bf m},P}\sim(\vee_{i=1}^{s-1}{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}c}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(Y_{red})_{+}\sim({{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n})^{\vee degP-1}.

Observe that these varieties are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-(n−1)(n-1)-connected smooth affine 2​n2n-folds. The problem of isomorphism classification is thus reminiscent of (a non-compact version of) that studied in [Wal62].

By an evident change of variables, we may assume that P⁡(z)P(z) is of the form z​Q​(z)zQ(z). When Q⁡(z)=(1−z)Q(z)=(1-z) and 𝐦=(1,…,1){\mathbf{m}}=(1,\ldots,1), the variety Q𝐦,PQ_{{\bf m},P} is the quadric Q2​nQ_{2n} whose 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type was studied in [ADF17] and the above construction gives another view of the proof of [ADF17, Theorem 2]. When Q⁡(z)Q(z) is general and 𝐦=(1,1){\mathbf{m}}=(1,1), the variety Q𝐦,PQ_{{\bf m},P} was studied implicitly in [AD08, Proof of Corollary 3.1] as a generalization of a construction of Winkelmann.

The following question can be viewed as a concrete generalization of the discussion of Remark 4.2.4 in the context of Example 4.2.5.

Question 4.2.6.

In the situation of Example 4.2.5, if PP is fixed, then can one distinguish non-isomorphic varieties of the form Q𝐦,PQ_{{\bf m},P} as 𝐦{\bf m} varies?

Remark 4.2.7.

For specific integral domains kk, the condition on P⁡(z)P(z) in Example 4.2.5 can be rather stringent. For example, if k=ℤk={\mathbb{Z}}, no polynomial of degree >2>2 satisfies the hypotheses. Indeed, given PP as in the statement of degree ≥3\geq 3, there exist 22 roots in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} that must differ by ≥2\geq 2. The standard expression of the discriminant as a product of differences of roots then shows that disc⁡P\operatorname{disc}{P} takes values in ℤ∖{−1,0,1}{\mathbb{Z}}\smallsetminus\{-1,0,1\}. As such, there exists a prime pp such that Spec⁡k⁡[z]/P\operatorname{Spec}k[z]/P has bad reduction modulo pp.

4.3 Constructing 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes

The discussion of the preceding section also gives a way to produce many new examples of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible strictly quasi-affine schemes generalizing the analysis from [ADF17, Theorem 3.1.1]. These provide new instances of exotic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible schemes (i.e., not isomorphic to affine k-spaces).

Proposition 4.3.1.

Consider the morphism π:XI,𝐚→𝔸kn\pi:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} from Proposition 4.2.2 where I⊂k⁡[x1,…,xn]I\subset k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] has height ≥2\geq 2, the morphism π\pi is smooth and Yr​e​dY_{red} is smooth over kk. Define EjE_{j} to be the closed subscheme corresponding to the ideal (I,∏i≠j(z−ai))(I,\prod_{i\neq j}(z-a_{i})) and set Xj:=XI,𝐚∖EjX_{j}:=X_{I,{\bf a}}\smallsetminus E_{j}.

  1. 1.

    The scheme XjX_{j} is a strictly quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme.

  2. 2.

    The morphism π′:XI,𝐚→𝔸s​Yn\pi^{\prime}:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Proof.

Proposition 4.2.2 implies that the morphism πj\pi_{j} is smooth and surjective. Moreover, by the construction of EjE_{j}, the base-change of πj\pi_{j} along the closed immersion Y→𝔸knY\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is simply the projection morphism 𝔸Yn→Y{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{Y}\to Y because EjE_{j} consists precisely of all but one of the components of 𝔸Y′n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{Y^{\prime}}. In particular, the morphism πj−1​(Y)→Y\pi_{j}^{-1}(Y)\to Y is always an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Corollary 3.1.4 thus guarantees that XjX_{j} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible if Yr​e​dY_{red} is smooth. Note that XjX_{j} is quasi-affine but not affine under the hypothesis that II has height ≥2\geq 2.

For the second statement, observe that each of the morphisms πj\pi_{j} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Since π′\pi^{\prime} is the pushout of all the morphisms πj\pi_{j} along their intersections, it follows that π′\pi^{\prime} is also an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, which establishes the second point. ∎

Remark 4.3.2.

Since Yr​e​dY_{red} is smooth, we may apply homotopy purity to describe the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of 𝔸s​Yn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY} along the lines of the final statement in Lemma 4.2.3. The corresponding statement is slightly more complicated because the normal bundle to Yr​e​dY_{red} in 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} need not be trivial. Of course, if Yr​e​d→𝔸knY_{red}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a codimension cc complete intersection, then the normal bundle comes equipped with a trivialization and then

XI,𝐚∼𝔸s​Yn∼(∨i=1s−1ℙ1∧c)∧(Yr​e​d)+.X_{I,{\bf a}}\sim{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY}\sim(\vee_{i=1}^{s-1}{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}c}){\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}(Y_{red})_{+}.
Remark 4.3.3.

In contrast with the situation for principal ideals II considered in Lemma 4.2.3 (1), Proposition 4.3.1(1) implies that when II has height ≥2\geq 2, the morphism π′:XI,𝐚→𝔸s​Yn\pi^{\prime}:X_{I,{\bf a}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY} is not an affine morphism. This observation has consequences for a higher-dimensional variant of the Danielewski fiber product construction. Indeed, suppose I′⊂k⁡[x1,…,xn]I^{\prime}\subset k[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] is another ideal corresponding to a closed subscheme Y′⊂𝔸knY^{\prime}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k}, and assume Yr​e​d′=Yr​e​dY^{\prime}_{red}=Y_{red}. Choose 𝐚′{\bf a}^{\prime} such that XI′,𝐚′→𝔸knX_{I^{\prime},{\bf a}^{\prime}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is smooth. In that case, we may form the fiber product XI,𝐚×𝔸s​YnXI′,𝐚′X_{I,{\bf a}}\times_{{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{sY}}X_{I^{\prime},{\bf a}^{\prime}}. One may show that either projection is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence, again by appealing to Corollary 3.1.4. Nevertheless, neither projection is affine since π′\pi^{\prime} is smooth and surjective, and the affineness of a morphism is local in the fppf topology on the base. As a consequence, neither projection can be Zariski locally trivial.

Example 4.3.4.

With the same notation as in Proposition 4.3.1, assuming that kk is a normal domain, then the isomorphism type of XjX_{j} is closely tied to the stable isomorphism type of YY. Indeed, take two 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibles as above, say XX and X′X^{\prime}, defined by subschemes YY and Y′Y^{\prime} (together with the choices of corresponding aia_{i} and ai′a_{i}^{\prime}). In that case, the normality assumption guarantees that an isomorphism between XX and X′X^{\prime} extends to the hypersurfaces X¯\bar{X} and X¯′\bar{X}^{\prime} in which XX and X′X^{\prime} are open subschemes, and then restricts to an isomorphism Y×𝔸r≅Y′×𝔸rY\times{\mathbb{A}}^{r}\cong Y^{\prime}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{r}. Thus, if YY and Y′Y^{\prime} are not stably isomorphic, the varieties XX and X′X^{\prime} are not isomorphic. Since non-isomorphic smooth curves of genus g>0g>0 are never stably isomorphic, by choosing non-isomorphic smooth curves of genus g>0g>0 in 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}, we may produce many non-isomorphic 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes. This produces many (e.g., positive dimensional moduli spaces) non-isomorphic strictly quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes of dimension d≥4d\geq 4.

Question 4.3.5.

Assume kk is a base ring. If Yr​e​dY_{red} is not necessarily smooth, then is XjX_{j} still an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence? More generally, if π:𝔛→𝔸kn\pi:\mathfrak{X}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is a smooth morphism of kk-schemes whose fibers over closed points are affine spaces, is π\pi an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence?

4.4 Topological contractibility revisited

In [AØ19, Conjecture 5.3.11], the first and third authors conjectured that if XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine variety, then Σℙ1n​X\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible for some nn sufficiently large and that n=2n=2 was probably sufficient. In view of Theorem 4.1.1, this conjecture can be made significantly more precise; the following proposition provides a non-conjectural result inspired by this circle of ideas.

Theorem 4.4.1.

Assume kk is a field having characteristic 00, and (X,x)(X,x) is a pointed H​ℤH{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth kk-affine variety.

  1. 1.

    For any integer N≥2N\geq 2, any smooth model of ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme; if XX is furthermore 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, then N=1N=1 suffices.

  2. 2.

    If XX is a topologically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth complex surface, then for any integer N≥2N\geq 2, ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X has the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme.

  3. 3.

    If XX is given as the vanishing locus of a hypersurface defined by f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], then for any integer N≥2N\geq 2 (or 11 if XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected) and any NN-tuple of integers (a1,…,an)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}) the hypersurfaces

    ∑i=1Nuiai​vi=f\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}^{a_{i}}v_{i}=f

    are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Proof.

For the first point, begin by observing that by appeal to Theorem 4.1.1 any suspension ℙ1∧s∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}s}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X admits a model as a smooth scheme. Next, pointed, smooth kk-schemes are H​ℤH{\mathbb{Z}}-local by appeal to [HKØ16, Lemma 4.1] (this argument appeals to resolution of singularities, which is where the assumption on the characteristic of kk appears). Then, arguing as in [HKØ16, Theorem 4.2], one observes that H​ℤH{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclicity guarantees that XX is ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-stably 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Next, if either N≥2N\geq 2, or N=1N=1 and XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, then ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X is at least 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-11-connected. By definition, ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X is at least 11-effective for N≥1N\geq 1 in the sense that it lies in the subcategory of Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} generated under homotopy colimits by spaces of the form 𝔾m∧U+,U∈Smk{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}U_{+},U\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k}. In that case [Bac21, Theorem 1.3] guarantees that since ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X is ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-stably contractible, it is already 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

For the second point, observe that topologically contractible smooth complex surfaces are H​ℤH{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic by [Aso11, Theorem 1]. That ℙ1∧N∧X{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}N}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}X is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible then follows from the first point and admits a smooth affine model by appeal to Corollary 4.1.6(2).

For the third point, we proceed as follows. Observe that if ff defines a smooth hypersurface in 𝔸r{\mathbb{A}}^{r}, then projecting onto 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} with coordinate uu and arguing as in Proposition 4.2.2 one concludes that the hypersurface ua​v=fu^{a}v=f is a model of the ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension of the hypersurface defined by ff. The result then follows by a straightforward induction. ∎

Remark 4.4.2.

If XX is a topologically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth complex surface, then XX is necessarily affine and if XX is not isomorphic to 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{{\mathbb{C}}} then XX necessarily has negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension [Zai99, Theorem 2.6]. On the other hand, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth surfaces are log-uniruled by [CR22, Theorem 4.7], so they necessarily have negative Kodaira dimension [KM99, Theorem 1.1]. It follows that topologically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth complex surfaces not isomorphic to 𝔸ℂ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{{\mathbb{C}}} are not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected.

Example 4.4.3.

Assume XX is a topologically ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic smooth complex surface. If XX has logarithmic Kodaira dimension 11, it was observed by Kaliman and Makar-Limanov [KML97, §7 Theorem on p. 606] that XX can always be realized as a hypersurface. Indeed, suppose k,l,mk,l,m are integers with k,l≥2k,l\geq 2, m≥1m\geq 1, g​c​d​(k,l)=1gcd(k,l)=1, and assume that f,g∈ℂ⁡[x]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x] are polynomials such that deg⁡f,deg⁡g<m\operatorname{deg}f,\operatorname{deg}g<m, f⁡(0)=g⁡(0)=1f(0)=g(0)=1, ff is arbitrary subject to the preceding condition and gg is uniquely determined by the condition that

pk,l,m,f​(x,y,z)=(zm​x+f⁡(z))k−(zm​y+g⁡(z))l−zzmp_{k,l,m,f}(x,y,z)=\frac{(z^{m}x+f(z))^{k}-(z^{m}y+g(z))^{l}-z}{z^{m}}

is a polynomial. In that case, the variety pk,l,m,f=0p_{k,l,m,f}=0 defines a topologically contractible hypersurface of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 11, and every such variety is isomorphic to a hypersurface of this form. In particular, Theorem 4.4.1 applies here, and we conclude that the hypersurface Xp,NX_{p,N} defined by

∑i=1Nui​vi=pk,l,m,f\sum_{i=1}^{N}u_{i}v_{i}=p_{k,l,m,f}

is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible for N≥2N\geq 2; this observation can be viewed as an improvement of [DPØ19, Corollary 3.7].

In the special case where N=1N=1, Kaliman and Zaidenberg observed that the resulting hypersurfaces could fail to be isomorphic to affine space [KZ00, Theorem 1]. We conclude from Remark 4.4.2 that the hypersurfaces pk,l,m,f=0p_{k,l,m,f}=0 are not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected and Theorem 4.4.1 does not guarantee the hypersurface Xp,1X_{p,1} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
